The famous achar menos etymology is unconfirmed: neither the DLE nor the DPD offers any origin for echar de menos, and the Wiktionary entry that does states it without a reference.

faqs.question: How do you say "I miss you" in Spanish in Mexico?
faqs.answer: Te extraño. It is the everyday form across Latin America, and the RAE's dictionary gives extrañar the sense "Echar de menos a alguien o algo, sentir su falta". Tatoeba sentence 436802 pairs Te extraño. directly with "I miss you."

faqs.question: Is "te extraño" romantic, or can I say it to a friend?
faqs.answer: Either. The RAE attaches no register or relationship restriction to the sense, and the Wiktionary entry's dated citation is Roberto Bolaño missing Russia and Moscow — places, not a partner. Tone comes from what you write around it, not from the phrase.

faqs.question: How do I say "I miss you so much" in Spanish?
faqs.answer: Te extraño mucho. (Tatoeba 1056427) in Latin America, or Te echo mucho de menos. (491227) in Spain. Note where mucho sits in the second one — it splits the idiom rather than following it.

faqs.question: What do I text back when someone says "te extraño"?
faqs.answer: Creo que yo también te extraño. is the attested reply form (Tatoeba 1737188, "I guess I miss you too"). The shorter Y yo a ti that most English-language lists print returned zero results when I searched the Spanish corpus, so it is not in this post.

faqs.question: How do you say "I'll miss you" before someone leaves?
faqs.answer: Te extrañaré mucho. — attested as "I'll miss you very much" (Tatoeba 767219). It is the future of the same transitive verb, so nothing about the grammar changes.

faqs.question: How do I say "we miss you" to one person?
faqs.answer: Te extrañamos. (Tatoeba 4788235). Only the verb changes; te stays singular because it still points at one person. For the past, Te extrañé. is "I missed you" (4484502).

faqs.question: Is "te echo de menos" only used in Spain?
faqs.answer: No. It is the ordinary form in Spain, but the RAE's own Diccionario panhispánico de dudas illustrates it with a Chilean novel, Collyer's Pájaros (1995). Treat it as a strong regional tendency, not a border.

faqs.question: Is "me haces falta" stronger than "te extraño"?
faqs.answer: It says something different rather than something stronger. The RAE files it under falta as "No tenerlo cuando sería necesario o provechoso" — not having someone when it would be necessary or useful, which is a claim about need. Many speakers hear that as heavier precisely because it is not about your feelings.

faqs.question: Does Spanish have a single word like the Portuguese saudade?
faqs.answer: Not one I could verify. The RAE lists añorar as a synonym under extrañar, but I did not fetch the añorar entry or check it against a corpus, so this post does not print it or claim an equivalent exists.

faqs.question: Should I write the whole message in Spanish or just the phrase?
faqs.answer: Just the phrase, unless you can read the reply. A Spanish line inside an English message reads as effort; a full Spanish page you cannot read back turns their answer into homework. Among 214 miss-you pages measured on 2026-09-25, the median letter is 88 words — one phone screen, which is about the right room for one foreign line plus two memories.

article.contentMarkdown:
# I Miss You in Spanish: Which of the Three Phrases to Send

"I miss you" in Spanish is **te extraño** across most of Latin America, **te echo de menos** in Spain, and **me haces falta** when what you mean is closer to "I need you". The Real Academia Española defines all three, and it marks neither of the first two as regional — that split is a habit, not a rule. Which one you send matters less than what you put around it. Across 214 "I miss you" pages built since 2026-07-28, the median letter runs 88 words and the longest is 1,024. Those senders are the most guarded group measured on the platform: 43.5% password-protect the page before sharing, against 38.5% platform-wide. Below, each phrase is graded against the RAE's own entry, every Spanish line is checked against an attested corpus, and the famous etymology is marked for what it is — unsourced.

## What te extraño, te echo de menos and me haces falta actually mean

All three translate as "I miss you", but they are three different sentences. *Te extraño* makes you the subject and the other person the object; *te echo de menos* does the same job through a fixed idiom whose verb no longer means what it looks like; *me haces falta* flips the grammar, so the other person is the subject and you are the one it happens to.

The RAE's [Diccionario de la lengua española entry for *extrañar*](https://dle.rae.es/extra%C3%B1ar) gives sense 2 as "Echar de menos a alguien o algo, sentir su falta" — to miss someone, to feel their absence. Its [entry for *echar*](https://dle.rae.es/echar) gives the locution two senses: "Advertir o notar su falta", and "Tener sentimiento y pena por su falta". The second one is the emotional reading.

*Hacer falta* is filed somewhere else entirely. Under [*falta*](https://dle.rae.es/falta), the lemma that matches "me haces falta" reads "hacerle a una persona falta alguien o algo: No tenerlo cuando sería necesario o provechoso" — not having someone when it would be necessary or useful. That is a sentence about need, not longing — the whole reason people argue over which is strongest.

## The three phrases, graded

Each entry states the same four things in the same order: dictionary sense, where it is used, what the grammar does, and when to send it.

### 1. Te extraño — the Latin American default

**Dictionary:** DLE *extrañar*, sense 2, "Echar de menos a alguien o algo, sentir su falta." **Where:** the everyday form across Latin America; Wiktionary labels the "miss" sense "(transitive, Latin America, otherwise formal)". **Grammar:** plain transitive — *yo* is the subject, *te* is the object, and the verb descends from Latin *extraneāre*, "to treat as a stranger", which the RAE prints at the head of the entry. **Send it when:** you want the neutral, unmistakable version. Attested: *Te extraño.* (Tatoeba sentence 436802), *Te extraño mucho.* (1056427), *¡Cuánto te extraño!* (7189421), *Mamá, te extraño.* (13378557).

### 2. Te echo de menos — the Spain standard

**Dictionary:** DLE *echar*, "echar de menos algo o a alguien", with the emotional sense spelled out as "Tener sentimiento y pena por su falta". **Where:** the ordinary form in Spain; Wiktionary labels it "(idiomatic, Spain, otherwise formal)". **Grammar:** a frozen locution. The [Diccionario panhispánico de dudas](https://www.rae.es/dpd/echar) calls it a "locución verbal transitiva" meaning "notar la falta [de alguien o algo]" and notes that the older variant *echar menos* "está hoy en desuso" — though it survives as its own DLE lemma, redirecting to the longer form. **Send it when:** you are writing to Spain, or want something a shade more literary. Attested: *Te echo de menos.* (454574), *¡Te echo de menos!* (10459224), *Te echo mucho de menos.* (491227).

### 3. Me haces falta — the one with no corpus attestation

**Dictionary:** DLE *falta*, "hacerle a una persona falta alguien o algo: No tenerlo cuando sería necesario o provechoso." **Where:** heard across the Spanish-speaking world, but it is the one phrase here I could not attest. Tatoeba's Spanish corpus returns fifteen *hacer falta* sentences for it and every one is third-person — *Me hace falta.* glossed "I miss it", *Me hace falta dinero.* glossed "I'm in need of money". Not one second-person hit. **Grammar:** the experiencer construction. *Tú* is the subject, *me* is the indirect object; literally "you make a lack to me". **Send it when:** you mean that their absence is a practical hole in your life, not only a sad one. It is the strongest of the three to many ears precisely because it is not a sentence about your feelings.

## How the three compare

The columns below mix dictionary facts with what the phrase actually does in a message.

| Phrase | RAE gloss | Regional habit | Grammatical subject | Attested in Tatoeba |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Te extraño | "Echar de menos a alguien o algo, sentir su falta" | Latin America | you (the sender) | yes — 7 lines checked, e.g. 436802 |
| Te echo de menos | "Tener sentimiento y pena por su falta" | Spain | you (the sender) | yes — 3 lines checked, e.g. 454574 |
| Me haces falta | "No tenerlo cuando sería necesario o provechoso" | both, informally | them (the person missed) | no second-person hit in 15 results |

The takeaway is the last column: the phrase most lists rank third has the thinnest evidence behind it.

## Where "echar de menos" comes from — and why the RAE will not tell you

Almost every page on this query repeats that *echar de menos* comes from Portuguese *achar menos*, "to find lacking", reanalysed as *echar*, "to throw". Here is the honest state of that claim.

**The RAE does not say it.** The DLE defines the locution without offering any etymology. The Diccionario panhispánico de dudas treats the phrase at length and also gives none; its normative energy goes elsewhere, ruling *echar en falta* "igualmente correcta" while discouraging *echar a faltar* as a calque of Catalan *trobar a faltar*.

**Wiktionary does say it, and cites nothing.** The [English Wiktionary entry](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/echar_de_menos) traces it to "an archaic and dialectal Old Galician-Portuguese idiom, *achar (de) menos*", entering Spanish by confusion of *achar* ("to find", Spanish *hallar*) with the similar-sounding *echar*. The Spanish Wiktionary says the same. Neither gives a reference. The authority usually named for it is Corominas, which is not online, which I could not fetch, and which I therefore do not cite.

Two corrections fall out. The source is **Old Galician-Portuguese**, ancestor of both Galician and Portuguese — not modern Portuguese. And "I throw you less" is the *result* of the mistake, not the origin: the original verb meant *find*. Any page presenting the throwing as the etymology has the arrow backwards. Treat the story as plausible, widely repeated, and unconfirmed by the Academy.

The regional split is softer than it looks too. The DLE prints *extrañar* sense 2 with no `Am.` marker, in an entry that does use markers elsewhere — and the DPD's own illustrative quotation for *echar de menos* is from a Chilean novel, Collyer's *Pájaros*, 1995. A tendency, then, not a border. Spanish has roughly 600 million speakers and, as the open-access dataset paper [*Spanish is not just one*](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12504998) (Data in Brief, 18 September 2025) puts it, "exhibits significant lexical, morphological, and syntactic variation across regions". I did not run a country-by-country frequency count, so I am not claiming one.

## What 214 miss-you pages say about the words around the phrase

Getting the phrase right is the small half of this. Measured on 2026-09-25 across the 214 pages built on the [miss-you page for a partner](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf):

The median letter is **88 words**, the longest 1,024. Eighty-eight words is about one phone screen — long enough for the Spanish line plus two specific memories, short enough to be read twice. 86.4% of those pages carry at least one written memory, 4.5 on average.

Recipients respond to gesture more than length. Across 138 of the 214 pages they tapped a "hug" 1,434 times, 512 of those on one page — receiver-side behaviour, and the number that changed how I would write one of these. Voice notes are rarer than you would guess: 13.6% record one, and 28.0% set a reunion date for the countdown.

Three limits on all of that, stated because they matter. The city, background-music and "together since" fields are **pickers with defaults**, so the 47 distinct city pairs those pages name — Mumbai–London and Berlin–London among them — come from a 15-city picker and are not free-text sender choices. The view figures behind those pages count page views, not unique visitors; one person reopening a page twenty times is twenty views. And n = 214 over two months, since the template went live on 2026-07-28, which is far too little to support any seasonal claim.

If the distance itself is the subject rather than the words, the [train-ticket letter page](https://subhsandesh.in/train-ticket) suits that reader better — built around a journey, a PNR and a running status rather than a paragraph, which fits the cross-border pairs above more closely. When a song carries it better than a sentence, the [radio dedication page](https://subhsandesh.in/dedication) is the honest alternative.

## When a Spanish phrase is the wrong thing to send

If your Spanish stops at the phrase, a Spanish-language page is a bad idea. The reply arrives in Spanish, and a page you cannot read back is worse than an English message that sounds like you.

Send English if the recipient is fluent in it and Spanish is their second language — the phrase then reads as effort, charming in one line and exhausting across a whole page. Send nothing digital if they are in the same city this week; 43.5% of these senders lock their page behind a password, which tells you this is a format for people genuinely apart, not for people who could show up.

And if the missing follows an argument rather than a distance, none of these three phrases is the sentence you need. *Te extraño* after a fight reads as avoidance.

## Sources

- Real Academia Española, *Diccionario de la lengua española*, entry **extrañar** — https://dle.rae.es/extra%C3%B1ar
- Real Academia Española, *Diccionario de la lengua española*, entry **echar** — https://dle.rae.es/echar
- Real Academia Española, *Diccionario de la lengua española*, entry **falta** — https://dle.rae.es/falta
- Real Academia Española, *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas*, 2nd edition, entry **echar** — https://www.rae.es/dpd/echar
- Wiktionary, **echar de menos** (etymology, unreferenced on the page) — https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/echar_de_menos
- Chiruzzo et al., *Spanish is not just one: A dataset of Spanish dialect recognition for LLMs*, **Data in Brief** 63, 18 September 2025, CC BY — https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12504998

Every Spanish line above was checked against the [Tatoeba corpus](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/436802); sentence ids are printed beside each one.

structuralLimitations: AGAINST THE LIVE HUB /blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages: the hub gives Spanish two lines inside a 50-language list ('Spanish (Latin America): Te extraño', 'Spanish (Spain): Te echo de menos') plus one FAQ repeating the same pair. Fetched 2026-09-25. It never mentions me haces falta, never names a dictionary, never touches grammar, register or etymology, and cites nothing. This post does not restate its table; it supplies the RAE and corpus layer underneath that one row. It also contradicts the hub on one point: the hub asserts that Spanish 'añoranza' captures deep longing in a single word, which I could not verify and therefore do not repeat.

AGAINST THE LIVE SIBLINGS: 81 live articles carry 'miss' in the slug, but zero are in Spanish. The nearest are i-miss-you-in-marathi, i-miss-you-in-tamil-words and how-to-say-i-miss-you-in-hindi. Language is one of the three never-duplicate axes in the BRIEF, so this is a new row and not a merge candidate.

PROMPT CLAIM CORRECTED — 'echar de menos … is widely traced to Portuguese achar menos'. Partly true, three corrections. (1) Every source that carries the claim says Old Galician-Portuguese / galaicoportugués, not modern Portuguese. (2) The RAE does not carry it at all: dle.rae.es/echar lemmatises the locution with no etymology, and www.rae.es/dpd/echar treats it at length with no etymology either. (3) The only fetchable sources stating it — en.wiktionary.org and es.wiktionary.org — give no reference for it. Corominas's DCECH, the authority usually named, is not online; I could not fetch it and do not cite it. Verdict printed in the post: plausible, widely repeated, unconfirmed by the Academy.

PROMPT CLAIM CORRECTED — the brief's gloss of echar de menos as 'literally I throw you less/short'. That is the literal reading of the reanalysed Spanish form, not the origin. Old Galician-Portuguese achar means 'to find' (from Latin afflāre, cognate with Spanish hallar, per en.wiktionary.org/wiki/achar), so the original sense was 'to find lacking'. Any page presenting the throwing as the etymology has the derivation backwards.

PROMPT CLAIM SOFTENED — 'the regional split … is documented'. What is documented is narrower than the prompt implies. dle.rae.es/extrañar prints sense 2 with NO Am. label, in an entry that does use p. us. and desus. elsewhere, so the DLE treats extrañar as general Spanish. The Spain/LatAm labels come from Wiktionary usage notes, not the Academy. And the DPD's own illustrative quotation for echar de menos is Chilean (Collyer, Pájaros, cl 1995). Reported in the post as a tendency, not a border.

NOT MEASURED, SO NOT CLAIMED: I found no country-by-country corpus frequency count for extrañar vs echar de menos. Searched via findpapers.mjs (Crossref + Europe PMC) on 'Spanish dialectal variation lexical choice', 'emotion concept translation bilingual' and 'long distance relationship communication maintenance'. RAE's CORPES XXI and CREA were not queried — no public JSON endpoint was reachable from this run. The post says explicitly that no frequency count was run.

SERP: one WebSearch run for 'i miss you in spanish', US-served, 2026-09-25, 9 results. Four are off-intent entity pages (Wikipedia film, Wikipedia telenovela/song, two Facebook posts). Three content pages probed for structure only: spanishdict.com (~857 tokens, 4 H2s), quillbot.com (~2,967 tokens, FAQPage schema, ~8 of its headings are product upsell), discoverdiscomfort.com (~2,413 tokens, 5 phrase H3s). No AI Overview was observed because the search tool does not expose one — no claim is made about it either way.

LINES CUT, not printed, because they could not be verified: 'Y yo a ti' — the standard reply on two competing pages; zero Tatoeba results and not a DLE lemma; the attested 'Creo que yo también te extraño.' (1737188) is printed instead. 'Te añoro' — añorar is listed by the DLE as a synonym under extrañar, but the añorar entry was not fetched and no attestation check was run. 'añoranza' as a single-word untranslatable — asserted by SubhSandesh's own hub, unverified here. 'Me haces mucha falta' — no lemma, no attestation. 'Ojalá estuvieras aquí' and 'Ya quiero verte' — competitor lines, no dictionary or corpus check run. 'Te extraño, mamá' — 0 hits in that word order; the attested 'Mamá, te extraño.' (13378557) is printed instead.

LINE PRINTED ON DICTIONARY EVIDENCE ONLY: 'Me haces falta.' It rests on the DLE falta lemma 'hacerle a una persona falta alguien o algo. 1. loc. verb. No tenerlo cuando sería necesario o provechoso.' A Tatoeba search for the exact second-person form returned 15 hacer falta sentences, all third-person. The post states this in prose rather than hiding it.

SOURCE READ DEPTH: the Data in Brief paper (PMC12504998) was read at abstract level, retrieved through the Europe PMC REST API. It is open access under CC BY and not paywalled, but the full text was not read, and the only claim taken from it is the sentence quoted in the body.

BATCH TOOLING BUG FOUND: content/batches/2026-09-25-miss-you-30/capcheck.mjs is a copy of the propose-30c version and still points at the wrong directories — HERE = 'content/batches/2026-09-24-propose-30c/blogs' and PRIOR = the three propose batches. Run as shipped it counts the wrong batch entirely and will report a clean cap for this batch no matter what is in it. I counted this batch's blogs/ directory directly instead. Whoever owns the batch should fix the two constants before the other five agents trust it.

failed.item: No section closely mirrors a competitor page's structure or framing
failed.why: The three H3s are named after the three phrases, which is the same top-level shape QuillBot and Discover Discomfort use. The four fields inside each H3 (dictionary sense, regional habit, grammar, attestation) are not theirs, but the section skeleton is a near-inevitable convergence on this keyword and it would be dishonest to call it independent.

The three graded H3 blocks run five to six sentences each, because the four-field format in references/page-structure.md packs dictionary sense, region, grammar and attestation into one block. Splitting them into 2-3 sentence paragraphs would break the field parallelism that makes them machine-extractable. Every other paragraph in the post is within range.

failed.item: At least one table column uses first-party data
failed.why: Structural, not fixable today. The comparison table's columns are all dictionary or corpus values because the miss-you segment records no message language — the /missyou-gf probes capture letter length, password use, hug taps and reunion dates, but nothing that could be broken down by which Spanish phrase a sender used. A first-party column would need a language field on the letter, which does not exist.

failed.item: 3–6 outbound links, all fetched and verified to contain the cited fact
failed.why: Seven unique outbound URLs, one over the literal cap. Five carry research claims (dle.rae.es x3, www.rae.es/dpd, europepmc.org); the other two, en.wiktionary.org and tatoeba.org, are the reference instruments this batch's verify.config.json exempts from the source cap, and the batch's own language-verification rule requires them. On the exempt reading the post is at five; on a literal count of body URLs it is at seven.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a specific reason to cite this: it is the only page on the query that quotes the RAE lemma by lemma, reports that the Academy gives echar de menos no etymology at all, and states that me haces falta returned no second-person hit in the corpus it checked — three verifiable claims the four competing pages do not make because none of them cites a dictionary or a corpus. The 214-page first-party layer (88-word median letter, 43.5% password use, 1,434 recipient hug taps) is unavailable to any language-learning site. Against that: spanishdict.com is a dictionary brand on its own home turf and quillbot.com already carries FAQPage schema, both on domains far above this one, and this is a US-market English query where SubhSandesh has no topical footprint in Spanish at all. Ranking takes months and I am not predicting one. What would most change the odds is a per-phrase first-party breakdown, which needs a language field on the miss-you letter that does not exist today.
